headline: Truck driver killing: Sheikh Hasina and 33 others indicted
summary: A special court in Dhaka has framed charges against the deposed prime minister and other former AL leaders in connection with the death of a truck driver during the July uprising.
details: A special court in Dhaka has framed charges against deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina and 33 others in a case linked to the killing of a truck driver during the July uprising.
The order was passed by Judge Md Rabiul Alam of the Special Judge’s Court-4 in Dhaka.
The case involves the death of 25-year-old truck driver Mohammad Hossain, who was killed in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur area during protests on July 19, 2024.
Eleven accused, including former ICT state minister Zunaid Ahmed Palak and former lawmaker Sadek Khan, pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Arrest warrants were issued against 23 absconding accused, including Hasina, Obaidul Quader, Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal, Mohammed Hasan Mahmud, and Jahangir Kabir Nanak.
The case was initiated following a murder case filed by the victim's mother, Rina Begum, on August 27.
According to court records and police, 920 cases, including 560 linked to killings, have been filed with different police stations in Dhaka alone until July this year.
caption:
Sheikh Hasina and 33 others have been indicted for the killing of a truck driver during the July uprising.

A special court in Dhaka has framed charges against deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina and 33 others in a case linked to the killing of a truck driver during the July uprising.

The order was passed by Judge Md Rabiul Alam of the Special Judge’s Court-4 in Dhaka.

The case involves the death of 25-year-old truck driver Mohammad Hossain, who was killed in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur area during protests on July 19, 2024.

Eleven accused, including former ICT state minister Zunaid Ahmed Palak and former lawmaker Sadek Khan, pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Arrest warrants were issued against 23 absconding accused, including Hasina, Obaidul Quader, Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal, Mohammed Hasan Mahmud, and Jahangir Kabir Nanak.

The case was initiated following a murder case filed by the victim's mother, Rina Begum, on August 27.

According to court records and police, 920 cases, including 560 linked to killings, have been filed with different police stations in Dhaka alone until July this year.

headline: Italy protests erupt nationwide over cost of living, housing crisis
summary: Thousands of young people and students have taken to the streets across Italy, protesting against rising living costs, housing shortages, and government policies. Recent demonstrations in Rome and Milan saw clashes with police and the use of tear gas.
details: Protests have swept across Italy, with thousands of young people, students, and citizens demonstrating against the increasing cost of living, a severe housing shortage, and government policies. Following a violent protest on October 17, new demonstrations occurred on Saturday, October 24, in major cities including Rome, Milan, Turin, and Bologna. While clashes with police, tear gas, and water cannons were reported, the widespread looting seen in the previous week did not reoccur.

According to Italy's Public Security Department, the identities of 4,292 individuals have been verified in connection with the protests and looting nationwide. 371 people were taken to police stations, and 9 were arrested, with charges brought against 87. Among those taken to police stations, 110 were minors and 69 were foreign nationals.

A movement called 'Movimento 17 Ottobre' (October 17 Movement) began gaining traction on social media in mid-October, using platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and online chat groups to call for youth participation in protests. The primary grievances cited by protesters include a significant increase in the cost of essential goods, fuel, and rent, which has not been matched by a rise in average incomes. The housing cost crisis is particularly acute for students and young professionals in major cities like Milan, Rome, and Bologna.

However, not all protests are part of the same movement. Labor unions, student groups, and anti-war factions are also holding separate demonstrations. Some protesters are demanding increased government investment in education and healthcare, alongside a reduction in military spending, arguing that the government prioritizes defense expenditure over addressing the economic struggles of ordinary citizens.

The core of the recent Italian protests lies in the uncertainty surrounding the future of the younger generation. Many within Generation Z feel they are being deprived of the economic security and social opportunities their parents' generation enjoyed. Similar discontent among young people across Europe is fueled by rising education costs, housing crises, precarious job markets, and the escalating cost of living.

Sabrina Briziola, national coordinator for the university students' organization 'Unione degli Universitari,' recently articulated demands for safe educational institutions, dignified employment, public healthcare, and social justice. She highlighted a key student concern: the need not only for access to education but also for quality education and subsequent employment opportunities.

Julius Fintelman, co-founder of 'European Correspondent,' told CNN that this escalating discontent is transforming into protests due to a pervasive feeling that European politics is failing to meet the expectations of the new generation. He also noted that concerns about job security are exacerbated by the potential impact of artificial intelligence on early-career employment.

Italy's recent protests share similarities with recent demonstrations in France, with both countries experiencing dissatisfaction over education quality, living costs, and the future prospects of young people. A student protest at a high school in Rome on October 7 began with a statement of solidarity with the French movement. However, the Italian government maintains that the situations are distinct.

Italian Minister of Education Giuseppe Valditara stated earlier this month that the situation in Italy is very different from France. Despite this, student organizations in both countries echo similar demands. Alice de Brito, vice-president of the French student organization UNEF, informed CNN that student organizations across Europe are sharing experiences and protest strategies. She identified increased public investment in education, universities, housing, and the future of young people as a common demand among protesters in various countries.

A notable feature of the recent protests is the rapid dissemination of information and mobilization via social media. Organizers of the 'October 17 Movement' planned to announce the exact location of the October 24 protests at the last minute, creating logistical challenges for police in determining assembly points and security measures. The day before the protest, police conducted searches in 18 cities across Italy, identifying approximately 100 individuals suspected of involvement in the previous week's violence, nearly half of whom were minors.

In Rome, some protesters entered the historic Colosseum. Clashes occurred near the Quirinale Presidential Palace in the city center after protesters threw bottles at police. Authorities deployed water cannons to control the situation. In Turin, northern Italy, approximately four thousand people protested against militarization, facing police blockades.
